## **1 INTRODUCTION**

This report provides information, guidance and advice for staff of Scottish Natural Heritage (SNH) relating to the environmental, engineering and planning aspects associated with the development of offshore renewable energy projects.  Scottish Natural Heritage already has a policy stance w.r.t. renewable energy (SNH 2002a) and has recently produced a strategic locational guidance document for onshore wind farms in respect of the natural heritage (SNH 2002b) _._

The initial contract report was prepared for SNH by staff of Scott Wilson and this final report has been produced in collaboration with SNH’s Maritime Group.

The contract report was prepared over a five-month period in 2002.  Whilst details of technological developments and known environmental impacts were correct at time of writing, the offshore renewable industry is evolving in a rapid manner and changes to capabilities and design may occur over short timescales.

## **1.1 Background**

There is strong interest in the development of renewable energy technologies in general, and particularly power generation from ‘free’ resources such as wind, wave, water, tide and sun.  This interest is being encouraged by fiscal and policy initiatives at the global, UK and Scottish level to increase the proportion of electricity produced using renewable technologies.  The UK Government launched its new policy on renewable energy in 2000. The aim of the policy is to further stimulate the development of the UK renewable energy industry by setting an objective to provide 10% of the UK’s electricity requirements from renewable sources by 2010.  Scotland is well placed to achieve this target; currently around 13% of electricity is produced from renewable sources (principally hydro-power), rising to c. 18% by 2010 (http://www.scotland.gov.uk/library5/environment/renewenergy2010.pdf). The Scottish Executive has subsequently consulted on the development of renewable energy resources beyond 2010 and in particular on the principle of a target of 40% of electricity from renewables by 2020.  Scottish Natural Heritage considers that any targets for renewable electricity for 2020 should be accompanied by equally challenging targets for energy efficiency and demand reduction in the domestic and business sectors, and for containment or reduction of emissions in the transport sector (SNH _pers. comm_ ).  Whilst accepting that offshore generation plants are likely to be used to meet future targets, care should be taken to safeguard areas of natural heritage value and areas valued for their wilderness.

Most renewable technology development in the UK has taken place onshore, with hydro being the preferred method historically in Scotland.  However, wind power is increasing in importance as an energy source.  As the number of suitable sites onshore starts to decline (or becomes increasingly difficult to develop), attention is starting to turn to the offshore environment.

The Scottish Executive commissioned a review of Scotland’s Renewable Resources in 2001 (Garrad Hassan and Partners Ltd 2001).  This concluded that potential offshore resources (including wind, wave and tide) were large.  It was estimated that the resource might be capable of generating in the order of 46.5 GW in 2010.  The report noted that the existing grid on the west and north coast was acting as a limitation to exploitation.  Further work is required to understand and avoid conflicts and to identify constraints to development.

## **1.2 Development of advice**

Research and consultations have been the main tools used to prepare this report.  The research has involved a review of published and widely available documents related to renewable energy projects.  These include environmental statements, reviews and research reports.  Consultations have been held with relevant staff of SNH and other statutory agencies and developers.  A list of people contacted is contained in Chapter 18.

## **1.3 Purpose of report**

The overall objective of the report is to provide information for the development of best practice guidance for SNH staff use in current/future development proposals concerning offshore renewable energy projects.  Specifically the report aims to identify potential likely areas for offshore renewable energy developments; to review the natural heritage impacts of possible new offshore renewable energy projects and ancillary electricity transfer infrastructure requirements, e.g. the proposed west coast electricity connector cable; and to capture the experience gained from SNH participation in the establishment of previous projects to inform the preparation of best practice guidance. The information will be used in developing the SNH position on offshore renewable energy, which is currently underway.

## **1.4 Structure of report**

This report is divided into a number of sections.  The next section contains a number of chapters that describe the current state of development of different forms of renewable technology and the factors influencing their location.  The following section considers the factors that promote the development of offshore renewable energy projects (e.g. funding schemes), and how they are controlled.  The predicted environmental effects associated with the different forms of development are set out in the next section.  The final sections provide conclusions and recommendations and sources of further information.

## **STATE OF DEVELOPMENT OF THE TECHNOLOGIES AND DESIGN REQUIREMENTS**

## **2 OFFSHORE WIND ENERGY**

## **2.1 Description of the technology**

Wind energy is converted to electrical energy using turbines.  Offshore turbines are generally adapted from those used on-shore, but have been ‘marinised’ or made durable for the harsh environmental conditions encountered offshore.  Offshore wind turbines will typically be bigger, both in terms of physical size and generating capacity, and are generally more efficient, both because of the increased size and owing to the use of more advanced technology.  The principal differences in the technology are in the types of foundations, the installation of the foundations and the turbines, the increased importance of reliability and the accessibility of the machines in the harsh offshore environment.

Turbines are normally grouped into wind farms, and offshore wind farms will typically be larger than those on-shore due to higher connection costs etc.  Within each wind farm, the most aerodynamically efficient layout would be a single long line of turbines perpendicular to the prevailing wind direction, but in most typical developments the turbines would be arranged in a grid, oriented and optimised to make best use of the prevailing wind direction and yet minimise the length of cable runs and the associated electrical losses. For aerodynamic reasons the separation distance between individual turbines is critical and would typically be between five and eight rotor diameters, which equates to around 250 to 400 metres.

Each wind turbine consists of:

- A foundation;

- A tower;

- The nacelle;

- The hub and blades.

Foundations may be either gravity structures or piled systems, but virtually all offshore wind farms (either existing or  planned) use monopiles.  Gravity foundations provide stability to the tower through their self-weight,  are normally made of concrete, and are founded on a stable stratum at or below seabed level.  Piled systems may be either monopile (a single steel tube directly below the tower, placed by driving or in a bored hole) or a tripod system (a threepronged steel structure, held down to the sea bed by smaller, driven piles).  By far the most common foundation type at present is the monopile.  These can be up to 6m in diameter and, depending on seabed conditions, may have as much as 40m embedded length (although this may be less, e.g. 20m).  They are installed using conventional offshore oil and gas industry techniques.

The tower is essentially a hollow steel tube, tapered in cross-section, and some 60m to 90m or more in height.  It may be either bolted or welded to the foundation.  An access platform and doorway into the tower is provided at a point above high sea levels.  Inside each tower are located some of the controls and electrical connections.  Access ladders lead from the lower level up to the nacelle.

The nacelle is generally an elongated shell, located on top of the tower.  It houses the bearings that provide a rotating connection to the tower, the gearbox and generator, and the main drive shaft from the hub.  Access to the nacelle may either be from below through the tower, or through hatchways from above.

The hub connects the blades to the drive shaft, and allows control of the blade angle.  All current designs use three-bladed turbines.

_**Figure 2.1 Installation of wind farm at Blyth.**_ Picture reproduced by kind permission of AMEC Border Wind

Whilst current wind farms have used blade lengths of approximately 60m, most developers are planning to use the new generation of big turbines (i.e. anything up to about 3.5MW capacity), specifically designed for offshore operation.  These typically have rotor dimensions in excess of 100m and hub heights of about 80m (giving a maximum blade tip height of more than 130m).  The proposed wind farm at Robin Rigg (Natural Power 2002) is for turbines which have an installed capacity of 2–3.6MW, rotor height of 80m (above Mean Sea Level, MSL), and blade length of 50m to produce a maximum height MSL to blade tip of 130m.  The turbines will be installed using either a monopile, 5.5m in diameter, and to a depth of 35m, or a multiple foundation comprising three piles approx. 1.2 to 1.8m diameter and a depth of 35m.

Normally each turbine has its own transformer located either in the base of the tower or on the external access platform, and individual turbines are connected together using armoured sub-sea cables, typically at 33kV. Some wind farms are connected directly to an onshore substation at this voltage (via one or more sub-sea cables), although in many cases the substation is located at the wind farm itself, either on one of the turbines or more usually on a separate foundation structure. This substation contains protection and switching equipment and transformers that increase the electrical voltage (to 132kV or higher) for transmission to the shore.  At Robin Rigg it is proposed that each turbine will have a transformer at its base to transform the generated energy from 690 V to 33 kV.  Two cables at 132kV capacity will link the substation to the shore.

Offshore wind farms will also have at least one separate wind monitoring mast, which will typically be an un-guyed steel mast mounted on its own monopile foundation to carry anemometers and other instrumentation, located at the same height as the wind turbine nacelles.

From the wind farm, electricity cables run to the shoreline, and shore-based control facilities. From there, overhead or buried cables would be used to connect the wind farm to the national grid.

Other ancillary facilities associated with offshore wind may include the development of support industries for the manufacture or assembly of wind turbine components.  An example of this is the current move to re-open the Arnish fabrication yard on the Isle of Lewis to provide wind turbine towers.  Although the primary market for towers from this facility would be the proposed 300MW onshore wind farm for Barvas Moor on Lewis, this facility could also supply to offshore wind farms around the Scottish coastline.

## **2.2 Current Projects**

The move to offshore wind farms began in Denmark, Sweden and Holland with four demonstration wind farms built between 1991 and 1997.  There are now a total of 75MW of offshore wind power installed in Europe, with 4MW in the UK generated from a single location (Fletcher 2001).  This site, Blyth Offshore, is located 1km from the shoreline near Blyth (Northumberland) and represents the only operational offshore wind farm in the UK at present (October 2002).  It comprises two 2MW turbines at this location, and these are located on piles driven into a permanently submerged rock bed.  Depths of water vary between 6m (at low tide) and 11m (at high tide), and waves of up to 8m in height are expected at the site.

There are at present 20 offshore wind farm projects in pre-planning and planning stages around the coastline of the UK (see Chapter 15), two of which have already received all necessary consents and capital grants from the DTI.  Some of these are effectively on the same or adjoining sites (see www.crownestate.co.uk for an up-to-date list).  Of relevance to Scotland is the Robin Rigg wind farm proposal, to be located in the Solway Firth.  A final decision is awaited on the outcome of the application to construct and operate a wind farm on the site.  At least two further wind farms have recently been granted planning permission in UK waters.

Scroby Sands offshore wind farm will be sited off Great Yarmouth on the Middle Scroby Sands.  The project was awarded statutory consents by the DTI, DEFRA and DTLR in April 2002 (www.powergenrenewables.com/scrobysandsproject).  Powergen propose to install and commission the wind farm during 2003.  The nearby Cromer offshore wind farm development proposal meanwhile cleared another planning hurdle in January 2003 with the announcement that North Norfolk District Council members had decided the need for renewable energy overshadowed concerns for local fisheries (http://www.eeegr.com/newsmaster/t_news_info.php?refnum=194).  The council's joint development control committee voted unanimously in favour of the construction and operation of the windfarm, although final approval rests with the Government. If the Government gives the green light, construction of the windfarm will begin in 2003, and will be completed in six stages, with an expectation of being in operation by 2005.

The North Hoyle offshore wind farm will be located some 7.5 km off the North Wales coast between Prestatyn and Rhyl, and was granted consent by the Minister for Energy in July 2002 (www.npower.com).  National Power anticipate construction is due to commence in 2003.

## **2.3 Development Potential**

Offshore wind energy requires further demonstration and assessment before it can be considered to be a commercial technology, although it is fair to say that the technology is proven.  Although the success of onshore wind does provide some confidence, in the absence of demonstration projects using current technology exposed to the offshore environment, there remains uncertainty and risk, as well as substantial scope for cost reduction (Fletcher 2001).

The theoretical technical potential for electricity generation from offshore wind in Europe, is well in excess of predicted electricity demands.  Current indications are that areas around the Scottish coastline, along with those around Sweden and Denmark, have the largest offshore wind resources in Europe, averaging 9m/s at a height of 50m at 10km offshore (BWEA 2000).  By comparison, much of the English, French, Dutch and German coasts have an offshore wind resource of between 8 and 9m/s.  In general, the offshore wind resource diminishes from north to south.  Other constraints such as suitable water depths and seabed conditions, and proximity to grid connection points (as discussed below) means that this theoretical potential is unlikely to be realised.  However, many organisations believe that despite the problems the renewable energy can replace conventional power generation. Greenpeace for example have produced a ‘visionary plan’ highlighting the potential for offshore wind power that could be accessed of the East Anglian coast (AEA Technology Environment 2002).  The report identified that many actions need to be addressed now in order for prepare the way to realise the potential from offshore wind but even so enough electricity could be generated to meet a quarter of current UK demand.

The UK has extensive capabilities in the offshore arena from its involvement in the oil and gas industry.  Some of these skills are relevant to offshore wind e.g. project management, installation and maintenance, design and fabrication of large steel structures, cable laying and seabed surveying and soil sciences.  Although the majority of wind farm projects currently being proposed are restricted to relatively shallow water depths and are between 5 and 12 km from the shore, there may be some potential for developing wind farms associated with existing offshore oil and gas projects.  Some developers are apparently considering this, however, turbines would probably have to be on separate conventional foundations away from existing installations (oil and gas platforms are not designed for the sorts of loads imposed by turbines) and they would still need grid connection to shore (most platforms have stand-alone generating capacity for their own use), which would be very costly for all but the nearest oil and gas fields.

A major project is being considered by Talisman Energy Ltd on the site of the Beatrice oilfield beyond the territorial (12 mile) limit in the Moray Firth (DTI 2002).  The proposal is install up to 120 wind turbines, generating approximately 500MW and therefore providing 5% of the UK’s renewable energy needs (SNH _pers. comm._ ).  The company has launched a feasibility study to examine the technical and economic viability of the project.  Three sites in the north of Scotland have been provisionally identified as suitable options for connecting the offshore operation to the National Grid.  This includes the possibility of linking a site to the Beatrice oil field (SNH _pers. comm._ ).  The wind data for the area would determine the size of the turbines required.  If the project is to go ahead it could be in the region of five years before the first power is produced.  Placing turbines close to oil platforms has some advantages, mainly that there is existing infrastructure in place linking the production site to the mainland.  Turbines would not be placed on oil platforms, but would be located in the vicinity after the productive life of the oil field has declined.  Electricity cables could then be run along the existing oil pipelines to the shore.

Cost is likely to act as the practical limit to the development of the UK offshore wind resource.  The economics of offshore wind are expected to result in machines becoming

significantly larger than those deployed onshore.  Recent estimates of the cost of generation costs  from different types of energy generation plant are contained in the PIU Energy Review and a report by an inter-departmental analysts group, both published in February 2022 (www.cabinet-office.gov.uk/innovation/2002/energy/report/index.htm and www.dti.gov.uk/energy/greenhousegas/index.shtml).  The PIU estimated the costs of gasfired generation ( 2 – 2.3 p/kWh), new nuclear build (2.5 – 4 p/kWh), onshore wind (1.5 – 2.5 p/kWh) and offshore wind (2 – 3 p/k/Wh).

The other limiting factor for realisation of offshore wind potential is the capacity of the Scotland-England interconnecting grid.  There are suggestions of a new high capacity cable to be laid down the west coast, to supply the main (English) electricity market from the Barvas Moor and other possible projects on the west coast (http://www.dti.gov.uk/NewReview/nr51/html/back_page_art.html).  There have also been recent suggestions in the press of an east coast cable from Inverness down to the south of England ( _Scottish windmills to power London_ , Sunday Times, page 16, 17 November 2002).

In summary, the UK Government has underpinned its commitment to renewable energy with a series of support schemes designed to bring forward technologies at the demonstration stage. These are being provided through capital grants awarded through the DTI.  Further details are found in Chapter 7.  Scotland and the UK are well placed to develop further offshore wind farm technologies, and to make a significant contribution to achieving UK and European targets for renewable energy production and the reduction of ‘green-house’ gas emissions.

## **2.4 Factors influencing the location of a wind farm**

Current technology requires offshore wind farms to be built in relatively shallow water depths and reasonably close to the shore.  Various other factors influence the siting of a wind farm including effects on shipping, fisheries, wildlife, defence interests and visual acceptability (particularly in shallow areas close to the shore).  Whilst access and wave height become more important in remoter sites.  In the first round of offshore wind farms in the UK the distances from the have been constrained by current legislation, which only allows development in territorial waters (i.e. no further than 12 nautical miles from the shore).  Only in the Northern Ireland site did procedures stipulate a distance greater than five kilometres from the shore (Crown Estate 2002).  Some of these and other factors are considered below.

## _2.4.1 Wind resource_

Offshore wind speeds are generally higher than those found over the nearby land.  This is mainly due to the differences in friction experienced by air moving across water compared to air moving across land.

A typical estimate is that at 10km from the shore wind speeds are on average 1m/s higher than those experienced at the coast (BWEA 2000).  This can give energy yields up to 30% higher than those currently experienced with near shore wind farms.  The wind also tends to be less turbulent, and air densities are typically higher, both of which contribute to higher turbine efficiencies on offshore sites.

The life-span of an onshore wind turbine or its components can be reduced due to excessive fatigue loading, which is caused by wind turbulence from surrounding geographical features (e.g. topography, local vegetation changes, buildings, etc.).  None of these features exist offshore, and therefore fatigue loading on the turbine will be reduced.  It is however noted that wind interaction with the sea surface (i.e. waves) is likely to produce some turbulence, as are the surrounding wind turbines in the wind farm, and it is current practice to make an allowance for this during design.

Wind shear (the variation of the direction and velocity of the wind with height) is lessened away from the influence of land.  This means that in offshore applications, the wind direction will be more uniform from the bottom to the top of the swept area of the turbine blades, enhancing the efficiency of energy conversion.

There is also a meteorological feature known as low level ‘jets’ which can occur under certain atmospheric conditions.  These jets represent an unstable airflow and cause wind speed to rise sharply with height.  It is anticipated that designers will have to take account of this feature when investigating potential sites.

## _2.4.2 Water depth_

The greater the depth of water, the more technically difficult and costly a wind energy development becomes.  Wind turbine installation is technically feasible in water depths up to 30m in depth (www.bwea.com), although current projects are all focussed in water depths less than 15m.  The turbines proposed for Robin Rigg will be in water that is 4 to 13m below MSL (Natural Power 2002).

## _2.4.3 Distance from the shore_

The distances from the shore of the first round of offshore wind farms in the UK have been constrained by current legislation, which only allows development in territorial waters (i.e. no further than 12 nautical miles from the shore).  The DTI’s consultation _Future Offshore_ (DTI 2002) which includes recommendations for a legal framework for future offshore development, to address shortcomings and enable development to take place beyond the limit of territorial waters.  The suggested way forward is to legislate to vest clearly the UK’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) rights in respect of a Renewable Energy Productive Zone with the Crown Estate or other appropriate body.

Another important issue is that of visual impact.

## _2.4.4 Visual impact_

_Future Offshore_ (DTI 2002) highlights the issue of visual impact as a potential area of concern.  The impact will depend on the distance offshore, weather conditions and the height above sea level from where the development is being viewed. _Whilst The Guide to Best Practice in Seascape Assessment_ (Hill _et al._ 2001) has been suggested as a methodology for assessing impact, CCW have further recommended in their reply to the consultants working for the DTI, that distance figures quoted by Hill _et al._ (2001) cannot simply be used to represent high, medium and low levels of visual influence of a man-made structure on a seascape, as the figures will depend on the scale of the individual development (CCW _pers. comm._ ).  Thus the limit of visual significance depends on the size (and layout) of the turbines and needs to be determined for the proposal in question.  As a starting point, and in particular for the Strategic Environmental Assessment proposal in question, CCW suggested that for wind turbines at sea, 0 - 8 km, 8 –13 km and 13 – 24 km are suggested to represent distances for high, medium and low significant visual impact for wind turbines based on approximately 100 m high turbines.

Visual impact of the Robin Rigg proposal was the major issue and is likely to be for many of the future sites.  Even the Beatrice proposal in the Moray Firth, despite being beyond the 12 mile limit still has the potential for visual impact given its ability to be seen from either shore of the Firth depending on the weather conditions.

## _2.4.5 Wave conditions_

There are two factors that require to be considered in regard to wave conditions.  The first is the extreme wave heights, and the second is the form of the wave (e.g. an offshore swell wave compared to a near-shore breaking wave).

With regard to wave heights, early wind turbine installations were located in fairly shallow water with wave heights in the region of four to eight metres.  As construction depths increase, so too will the maximum wave heights.  Wave heights represent an undulation in the sea level and therefore, create a larger force on one side of the turbine than the other, thereby creating an overturning moment that has to be resisted by the turbine’s foundations and ultimately the seabed.  During design it is noted that the form of the wave (i.e. deep water or shallow water characteristics) is as important, if not more so, when examining wave loading on the structure (see comments below).

With regard to the form of the wave, this is related to the depth of water and the slope of the seabed in the area of the turbine.  Large forces are present in areas where waves are in the process of breaking, particularly in the form known as a ‘plunging breaker’.  Breaking waves will form at a structure when the seabed slopes up towards the structure and the depth of water around the structure is approximately equal to height of the incoming waves.  Wind turbines would require to be designed either to resist these forces or located outside of zones where large breaking waves would be expected.  It is noted that these zones will move depending on the height of the tide at a particular time.

## _2.4.6 Seabed materials_

As mentioned earlier, offshore wind turbines have either gravity or piled foundations.  The main constraints in regard to the use of gravity foundations relate to wave and tide action on and around the base of the structure, which can cause scour and possibly lead to undermining of the foundation.  Scour protection works would require to be designed around the base of each foundation to resist these forces.  The use of such foundations should be avoided in areas with fast tidal currents, areas prone to breaking waves, loose or shifting sand or soft clays.  Alternatively, piled foundations could be used (typically monopiles).  The main constraints to their use are again on areas of shifting sands or in areas where clay and boulders are present beneath the seabed, which cause technical difficulties during piling operations.

## _2.4.7 Navigation_

During construction and operation, wind farms would restrict the navigational passage of large vessels in the vicinity of each development.  It is also likely there would be some form of safeguarding zone around the wind farm to keep large vessels at a safe distance and thereby reduce the risk of a collision.  At present, most of the proposed sites are in shallow water and thus have little impact on major commercial shipping routes, but may have some limited effect on local and recreational use, and on the movement of fishing vessels.

If sites are located further offshore, then these wind farms would need to be located at a suitable distance from existing major shipping lanes, which for operational reasons cannot be moved.  However, it may be possible to re-route minor shipping lanes, e.g. those to and from small ports and harbours, around the wind farms.

Current thinking suggests that smaller (leisure) craft could navigate considerably closer to the turbines, and even between them assuming sufficient depths, although there may be a security restriction around the base of each turbine. The Royal Yachting Association in particular have raised concerns about proposal for dealing with the safety and navigation of

small vessels and recreational craft.  In their submissions to the Scottish Parliamentary Committee assessing the Robin Rigg, Solway proposal to create an exclusion zone of 50 m for such craft, the RYA argues that this was unnecessary, impractical and undesirable.  The RYA consider that in both the constructional phase and the operational lifetime, any wilful disruption should be dealt with through an interdict.

Most current proposals include provision for new buoyage lights and other local navigational aids and most Environmental Statements include a shipping collision assessment if the site is close to a major navigable route.

## _2.4.8 Fishing and fisheries_

All Environmental Statements completed for offshore wind farm developments around the UK have included some form of Fisheries Impact Assessment.  However, the need for ‘a strategic fisheries study aimed at identifying the specific effect of offshore wind farms on various types of fishing techniques and fisheries activities’ (ETSU 2000) has been identified.

Depending on the site selected, the immediate area occupied by wind farms may not be important for fisheries, or may occupy a significant proportion of the area normally fished. Fisheries may be affected during construction by increased turbidity and noise disturbance, although so far long-term impacts have been described as negligible and of minor significance (www.gunfleetsands.co.uk).

The DTI has established a Fisheries Liaison Group (England and Wales) to encourage open dialogue between the offshore wind industry sector and the fishing industry (DTI 2002)

Other impacts upon fishing activities are discussed in Section 11.3.4.

## _2.4.9 Obstacles on the seabed_

The following areas have been identified as being unsuitable for development of a wind farm:

- Areas around existing undersea pipelines or cables – it is likely that there would be a minimum distance from such obstacles to the nearest turbine, specified by the owners of the pipeline or cable;

- Areas that are or have been used for dumping munitions or hazardous waste – again it is likely there would be a minimum safe distance required; because of disturbance of the seabed during construction, and the potential environmental consequences of releasing toxic materials or causing an explosion.

Some areas of the seabed may also be contaminated as a result of historical activities. Consideration should be made of the risks of re-releasing these contaminants back into the environment (see Proceedings of the North-west ECSA meeting for more details: www.ecsa.org.uk).

It is also important that developers take account of areas of marine archaeological interest including ship wrecks and human artefacts

## _2.4.10 Military exercise areas_

There are currently a number of sea areas around the UK coastline that have restrictions to vessels because they are used as Navy exercise areas or firing ranges.  A wind farm development would require to be kept at a minimum safe distance from these areas.

Furthermore, MoD low flying zones extend out to sea in various locations, further restricting the location of wind farms.

## _2.4.11 Radar and communications_

A major constraint on the deployment of wind energy in the UK is the restriction on siting turbines due to the potentially hazardous effects they may have on aviation and related defence interests (Jago and Taylor 2002).  So far the MOD has indicated that it will object to five of the proposed 18 initial phase wind farm sites around the UK.  The reason identified is the interference caused to the radar system's of low flying jets by the movement of turbines.

Every major airport in the UK has safeguarding zones identified to prevent inappropriate developments that may affect their radar and communications with air traffic.  In addition, every airport within the UK has height restrictions for developments within a 15km radius.  If an airport is located on the coast these restrictions could apply some distance offshore. Outwith the 15km zone the main concern is the effect such a development would have on the aeronautical systems of air traffic control.  The degree of impact depends on the proximity of the development, the size and layout of the development, and the materials used.  Each development would require to be assessed on a case-by-case basis in this regard.

The Scottish Executive has undertaken a consultation exercise on the safeguarding of airports and other technical sites in Scotland.  This culminated in the issue of ‘Safeguarding Aerodromes, Technical Sites and Military Explosives Storage Areas:  The Town and Country Planning (Safeguarded Aerodromes, Technical Sites and Military Explosives Storage Areas) (Scotland) Direction 2001’, which gives guidance on the production of safeguarding maps for each Aerodrome and Technical Site in Scotland.  This document identifies a 30km radius around a civil technical site, within which any wind farm development requires consultation. Safeguarding maps for the aerodromes themselves are prepared with consideration of sitespecific issues, and therefore, no set radius is identified.  In areas where there are intensive shipping movements, then offshore wind farms may also have an impact on offshore traffic control and collision avoidance radar systems.

Jago and Taylor (2002) reported two issues of concern, largely not commented on in the UK but preoccupying many stakeholders in other countries:

1. Search and Rescue operations (SAROps) in the vicinity of large wind farms, particularly offshore; and

2. How best to mark and illuminate wind farms.

Although a UK policy is being developed to address the second of these concerns, it is reported that the responsibility for search and rescue within wind farm boundaries is something that has to be established.  Given the scale of some of the proposed offshore wind farms, SAROps would be required at some stage within the boundaries of such a development but this would be an extremely hazardous operation to undertake.

## _2.4.12 Areas used for dredging_

There are currently a number of licences issued by the Crown Estate for the extraction of offshore sands and gravels from designated offshore areas.  These licences are granted for areas of the east coast, south coast and the Bristol Channel.  These areas would clearly be unsuitable for development of a wind farm due to the constant changes to the seabed caused by extraction, and the attendant effects this would have on any foundations.

There are two such sites within Scotland currently licensed for aggregate extraction. Demand is relatively low but a licence has been granted for commercial sand extraction in the Firth of Forth at Middle Bank (though extraction has yet to commence here).  There is

also a site currently being worked for aggregate extraction in the Tay estuary.  The operators are Westminster Gravel Ltd and Scottish Aggregates Ltd., respectively, and the Scottish Executive Development Department, Planning Division is the responsible authority (SNH, _pers. comm_ .).

## _2.4.13 Nature conservation areas_

A detailed consideration of potential impacts associated with wind farm developments is provided in Chapter 11.

As for any form of development, the presence of designated areas of sea, or areas supporting protected species, are considered during the site selection process.  Additionally developers should seek to take note of the wider natural heritage beyond the confines of such designated sites and the wind farm location can be affected on a local scale by the presence of important habitats/species for which there may be no site designations present, e.g. those identified as a priority under the BAP process.  In general terms, the footprint of each turbine, particularly where a monopile foundation is used, is relatively small and therefore the impacts on the seabed and surrounding area are fairly localised.  It is not considered that such installations would present any significant long-term problems in regard to pollution of the surrounding area, as there are no discharges from such installations. However, localised disturbance of the seabed will take place during construction, and the physical presence of the foundations and sub-sea cables may have some impact on local seabed conditions, although all of these implications are normally covered in the EIA undertaken for each proposal.

Particular ecological concerns related to wind farms include impact of noise during construction upon mammals, impact of turbines upon bird populations during operation, and impacts upon sediment movements.  Landscape and visual aspects are also a concern, particularly for sites close to the shore (see Chapter 11).

As part of the ongoing work in this area offshore wind farms and designated areas was the subject of a European workshop, during January 2003 in Brussels, entitled _Natura 2000: Practical consequences of the EC’s Birds Directive and Habitats Directive for offshore wind farms_ .  The outcome of which was to highlight a series of key issues for further consideration (EN _pers. comm._ ):

- Co-ordinating assessment including cables;

- Knowledge, managing risk, precaution;

- Government policy/strategy, SEA

- Monitoring and evaluation;

- Mitigation and compensation;

- Sea use planning and information systems to underpin this;

- Species protection;

- Cumulative effects; and

- Interplay between public and private bodies.

## _2.4.14 Grid connection_

To minimise the grid connection costs, locations are sought as close as possible to the shoreline, consistent with visual impact and other considerations.  The Robin Rigg proposal lies approximately 9km from the Scottish coastline (and 12km from the English coast), whilst the site at Blyth is only 1km from the shore.

Current research indicates that connection of an offshore wind farm to the grid can account for between 17–34% of the overall project cost (BWEA 2000).  The higher end of this cost

bracket is achieved when wind farms are furthest from the shore, thereby requiring long lengths of cable to connect to the grid, and the infrastructure on the shore also needing to be improved to accept the additional power.  It is envisaged that large wind farms will require power connection at either 132, 275 or 400kV onshore.  This could mean high costs associated with upgrading the electricity transmission supply network in more remote coastal areas, to accept the power from an offshore wind farm development.

Studies by ETSU into the capability of the current grid transmission system have shown that wind power generation of up to 10% of the peak demand, is unlikely to require any significant changes in operating procedures for the grid or additional equipment (ETSU 2001).  As wind energy approaches 20% of peak demand it is likely that additional reserve power sources (e.g. coal and gas), run on a stand-by basis, will be required to cope with the variability of wind energy.

Furthermore, the study by ETSU showed that East Anglia, Sussex, Kent and South Wales are all feasible areas for offshore development, as the transmission system in these areas is capable of accepting additional generation without extensive reinforcement.  Scotland, northern England and North Wales may have limitations in regard to the acceptance of additional generation due to the existing electrical infrastructure.  The report noted that 4GW of offshore wind energy is possible within the existing grid structure, provided that the sites are geographically dispersed.  Problems with ‘fault levels’, usually a low capacity for this in coastal areas, could be overcome by using existing generators (power stations but not nuclear) to moderate the energy from wind farm development.

The DTI highlighted the issue of grid connection in their _Future Offshore_ consultation (DTI 2002) indicating that ensuring that infrastructure is provided and priced efficiently is important for the success of the offshore wind strategy.  Further Brian Wilson (Minister for Energy and Construction) indicated in oral answer in the House of Commons (16 January 2003) that there “.. _is no point in generating electricity if it cannot be taken to the markets where it is required.  We have a strong infrastructure, but it is based largely on the old coal and steel economy.  If we are to have a much more distributed range of generation, we must have an infrastructure to match._ “.  In fact the _Future Offshore_ consultation includes the desire for views for example as to who should provide the cables and who should regulate offshore infrastructure?  The potential of developers owning or being responsible for the cable between the wind farm and the grid is a departure from on land and is a strategic issue which has implications for future expansion but also environmental impact in the longer term, e.g. effect on decommissioning of wind farms which have a shorter life-span than the cable (EN _pers. comm._ ).

Energy regulator Ofgem, in its press release 13/01/03 R/4, raised the wider issue of the challenge of ‘rewiring’ Britain which will arise from Government energy and environmental policies (http://www.ofgem.gov.uk/public/pn2003/4.htm).  One of the key issues facing Ofgem and the distribution network operators that was highlighted was the question of how to deal with uncertainty in the type, timing and location of new power generation

## _2.4.15 Socio-economic considerations_

The development of wind farms will require an associated service industry to support them through their life-span, particularly if there are a number of wind farms in close proximity to each other.  Access to port facilities is also critical.  Although the number of jobs required to help service and maintain offshore wind farms is not directly proportional to the number of wind farms, there will be a requirement for more trained staff.  If there is a critical mass of wind farms in one particular area it could be possible to consider a regionally based service industry, perhaps evolving from the oil and gas industry.  For example, as noted in section

2.1, there are proposals to redevelop capabilities from the Arnish fabrication yard on the Isle of Lewis.

## **2.5 Site selection**

Some of the factors influencing the selection of a site were highlighted above.  A report produced by Garrad Hassan and Partners for the Scottish Executive in 2001 identified several areas around the Scottish coast as potentially suitable for wind farm development. The basis of selection was water depth (< 30 m), distance from the coastline (> 5 km to minimise visual impacts), navigational risks and environmental designations.  This process identified the following areas as those that may become the focus for offshore wind development:

- The Solway Firth,

- Small areas around Arran, Kintyre Peninsular, Islay, Jura, Tiree, and the Outer Hebrides,

- Off the Moray coast,

- East of Dundee.

## **2.6 Seabed Ownership**

As owner of the seabed the Crown Estate plays an important role in the development of the offshore renewables industry by leasing areas of seabed.  The Marine Estate element of the Crown Estate consists of 55% of the foreshore (over 10,000 km) in the UK, approximately half of the beds of tidal rivers and estuaries , and almost the entire seabed out to the 12 (nautical) mile territorial limit.  The Marine Estates include the right to explore and exploit the natural resource of the UK continental shelf, with the exception of oil, coal and gas.  Leases will only be granted to schemes that hold all the necessary permissions and statutory consents.  An ‘Agreement for Lease’ is granted while studies (environmental impact assessments) are undertaken and once all consents are gained, a full lease is then granted (Crown Estate _pers. comm._ ).

## **2.7 Construction**

To date, installation of turbines has been undertaken using vessels designed for the offshore oil and gas industry or vessels used for salvage or other types of marine construction (e.g. harbour construction).  So far, the industry has found the use and modification of such vessels to be relatively expensive and not ideally suited to the purpose.  It is expected that specialist vessels will be designed and built to serve the industry as it expands.

Construction operations are undertaken either by ‘floating’ vessels or jack-up rigs depending on the conditions at the site.  Jack-up vessels are more suited to shallower sites, generally between 15 and 20 metres of water, with tidal ranges up to 8m and wave heights up to 6m. Jack-up vessels provide a better work platform in terms of not being affected by waves or tides, however they need calm conditions to relocate and need to be towed to site.  Also, it is sometimes necessary to use rock dumping to stabilise a rig especially in sandy, highly mobile sediments (due to scour around the rig’s feet (spud cans) (JNCC _pers. comm._ )). Floating vessels are affected by waves and tides (resulting in overall more down time during construction) but generally are faster between relocations, and more suited to deeper water sites.

Piling/foundation operations are completed first, and then the tower, nacelle and blades are lifted into position by crane.  Usually, the main crane is supplemented by a smaller crane, which is used to control the lift and stop the components from swinging.  Previously, both insitu component assembly and wholly completed unit lift methods have been used, although

the latter appears to have been more widely used a number of years ago when turbines were smaller.

Meteorological monitoring masts are installed in a similar way to the wind turbines, although the foundations are typically much smaller.

Depending upon local conditions, cables may need to be buried.  The method of burial will depend on local seabed conditions, and the different methods have varying cost and environmental implications.  Typically ploughing the cable in as it is laid causes least disturbance (often less than 1m wide), whilst air or water jetting (where high pressure jets are used to excavate a trench in sediments, often as the cable is laid) can affect an area up to 3-4m wide.  Air jetting creates more disturbance and is more expensive than water jetting. In some situations, scour protection (often in the form of large boulders or rubber mats) will be placed around the turbine foundations and on top of the buried cables at vulnerable points.

The level of burial will depend on cable size and voltage, and grid connection cables (i.e. to shore) will typically be at a higher voltage (132kV or above) than the onsite collection voltage (usually 33kV).  This is to minimise electrical losses in the transmission to shore.

Discussions with developers indicate that access to ports is not considered to be a constraining factor, as most major ports have suitable space for docking of vessels and lifting of equipment.  Obviously, the proximity to an appropriate port will affect the viability of the project to some extent, and will also help to reduce traffic movements and other impacts during construction.

## **2.8 Maintenance**

Typical wind turbines are designed to last 20-25 years, although given the higher specification of the offshore machines they may be capable of longer operating lives. However, most Environmental Statements indicate a 20–25 year project life (e.g. Robin Rigg), and decommissioning at the end of that period is often addressed in the consenting process.

Exact maintenance requirements will largely depend on turbine type, but offshore machines are designed specifically to minimise unscheduled maintenance and typically manufacturers quote twice-yearly scheduled service visits. Ideally, scheduled services will be undertaken during low-windspeed periods (both for ease of access and to minimise lost production) and there will inevitably be some unscheduled visits as well.  Maintenance includes annual tasks such as checking for scour around the foundation, and less frequent activities such as painting the area of foundations above sea level, and replacement of sacrificial anodes (approximately every 10–15 years) (Natural Power 2002).

Whilst helicopter access is possible (and some projects incorporate heli-decks, particularly if separate sub-station platforms are to be used), access to individual turbines will probably most typically be by small work boat for routine maintenance, although the proximity to a suitable harbour and other local conditions will have some bearing on access methods.

When major component replacement is necessary, then larger vessels and possibly even jack-ups will obviously be needed.

## **2.9 Decommissioning**

Options for decommissioning are still in the development phase; it is possible to remove the turbines, and some statements also include suggestions of removing part of the structure

and leaving the foundations in place, subject to legislative approval (Natural Power 2002). Foundations are designed for a specific turbine type and whilst in theory, and subject to design assessments, a similar machine could be bolted to the same base, the foundation design life (in terms of stress cycles and corrosion protection etc.) is normally the same as the original turbine.

Given that a wind farm will already exist in a particular area, and the associated grid connection will still be viable, it seems likely that sites will be reused either by installing new turbines and foundations, or for some other renewables generation project. However, it is very difficult to predict where technology will be in 25 years time and any new project will have to be assessed on the basis of present proposals, but assuming that current or future legislation will protect against unreasonable development.

Indications are that are decommissioning is likely to be the subject of the both the Crown Estate lease (in terms of when it should occur) and the FEPA licence (in terms of the manner in which it should occur).  Although the latter is issued to cover the installation of the structures legal advice suggests that elements pertaining to the decommissioning of the structures can also be included as part of any deposit conditions of the FEPA licence (FRS, MLA _pers. comm._ ).

## **3 WAVE ENERGY**

## **3.1 Description of the technology**

There are two principal types of wave energy converters currently being researched for production of electricity: offshore and coastline wave energy converters.

The offshore wave energy converters identified in the production of this report are:

- The ‘Pelamis’ wave energy converter, being developed by Ocean Power Delivery (www.oceanpd.com).  This device floats on the surface and is moored to the seabed by flexible cables.  The device consists of a number of cylindrical sections that are hinged together.  Wave action on these hinges is absorbed by hydraulic rams, which in turn pump high-pressure oil through hydraulic motors, which then drive electrical generators within each unit.  Each unit is attached to the seabed using only one connection point, thereby allowing the unit to swing so that it is always head-on to the oncoming waves.

- The ‘Wave Swing’ wave energy converter, being developed by A.W.S B.V. (Archimedes Wave Swing B.V.[1 *] ) (www.waveswing.com).  The prototype device sits on the seabed, but future development may see the device floating above the seabed whilst attached by mooring cables to the seabed.  This wave energy converter makes use of the changing pressure on a water column as a wave passes over, i.e. increased pressure when the crest of a wave is directly overhead due to the increase in height of the water column. The device acts like a piston with a buoyant plunger; the cylinder is pressurised with air and it is changes in air pressure that drive the electrical generator.

- The ‘Moored Buoy’ wave energy converter, being developed by Aqua Energy Group (www.aquaenergygroup.com).  The device floats on the surface and is moored to the seabed by cables.  The device uses the orbital motion contained within waves to drive a turbine located in the upper section of the device. (See Figure 3.1).

The following coastline wave energy converters devices/systems have been identified:

- The ‘Osprey Wave Energy Collector’ is a near-shore device operating on the Oscillating Water Column principle.  This device is located on the sea bed within one kilometre of the shore, and operates by allowing the water to oscillate up and down inside a partially submerged shell.  Thus a column of air within the parts of the shell above the water level is alternately compressed and decompressed, and this air pressure is used to drive ‘Wells Turbines’ (www.wavegen.com).

- The ‘LIMPET’ uses the same energy conversion mechanism as ‘Osprey’, but is designed to be located on the shoreline.

Ancillary development associated with wave energy installations would be similar to those required for off-shore wind farms, and would include:

- cable connections to the shore;

- control buildings and sub-stations, likely to be provided at the shoreline, rather than offshore; and

- port facilities for construction and maintenance of the energy devices.

## **3.2 Current Projects**

In the UK, three projects have already been awarded contracts under the Third Scottish Renewables Order (the first Renewables Order open to wave power), and the prices are comparable with the predicted electricity costs from the first offshore wind farms, although admittedly there is much greater experience with wind turbines derived from their widespread use onshore (Clarke and Michael, 2001).

The ‘Pelamis’ device, being developed by Ocean Power Development (OPD), is currently still at a stage where scale models are being tested at sea using small power vessels to temporarily locate the devices during tests (http://www.oceanpd.com).  The first full-scale prototype is to be installed at the new Marine Energy Test Centre in Orkney in 2003.  OPD also have a contract for 0.75MW project to be installed off Machir Bay on Islay.

The ‘Osprey’ device, being developed by Wavegen (UK), currently has a 0.5MW device installed on the coast of Islay, and has been operating since October 2000.

The ‘Moored Buoy’ device, being developed by AquaEnergy Group (USA), is due to have the first 1MW commercial plant installed in Makah Bay, Washington State, USA in August 2003.  However, much testing has been undertaken in the waters off the coast of Sweden during the 1990s.
