## **3.3 Development Potential**

The UK has one of the best wave power resources available (Clarke and Michael 2001). The power available in the waves is much greater offshore than on the shoreline.  This is because shoreline sites often fail to meet the requirement for useful energy capture.  Near the shore, energy from easterly winds is not available and bottom friction reduces power levels in depths less than 80 metres, so that inshore sites get only a quarter or less of the deep-water resources.  This reduction can be offset in some shoreline locations by the effects of refraction that can focus the wave energy creating locally attractive sites.

However, the engineering challenges of deep-water sites are different.  Transmission costs and losses will be higher for offshore sites than those onshore, but wave power is generally higher. Onshore sites are inaccessible in bad weather.

In general, shoreline wave energy conversion is technically developed but not fully commercially proven and is still some way from being truly commercially competitive. Furthermore, there is presently insufficient operating experience, and schemes need to demonstrate long-term performance and reliability.  Offshore wave energy is still mainly in the research and development stage, with much work needed to tackle key development issues, reduce uncertainty and verify the concepts.  However, as technology develops, the predicted costs will continue to be reduced.  Nonetheless, studies have shown that predicted energy costs from wave energy devices would still not be truly commercially competitive with electricity supplied from the grid at today’s costs, and so further innovation is required to overcome these challenges.  However, there may be earlier opportunities in supplying electricity to isolated or island communities, where the competition may be from diesel generation.

The report ‘Scotland’s Renewable Resource 2001’ (Garrad Hassan and Partners Ltd 2001) excluded the eastern seaboard of Scotland from consideration, since the available energy is an order of magnitude less than that of the western (Atlantic) seaboard.  The report focussed on areas with water depths greater than 40m, and which lie outside environmental designations and shipping routes.  The analysis showed that the best areas were westward of the Western Isles, from Mull up to the Outer Hebrides, as well as west of the Orkneys and Shetlands.  The most viable locations were thought to be those located in the vicinity of the Outer Hebrides.

In acknowledgement of this Brian Wilson, Energy Minister announced, in May 2002, Government funding of up to £2.3 million to support for Wavegen, based in Inverness, the development and demonstration of a series of new wave energy devices off the Western Isles (DTI News Release 20 May 2002, DTI/SCO/064/02).  The funding offer was to be based on three shallow water devices, based on an extension of the oscillating water column principles.  The proposal for a cluster of wave power devices for the Western Isles was - reported as being brought a step closer to reality (News@All Energy. Issue 18 January 2003) with the awarding of £3.7 million by Brian Wilson, as Wavegen and Tidal Hydraulic Generators Ltd have passed the necessary technical appraisal to take their projects from design stage to prototype.  Thus proving that the UK has world-class experience in the development and evaluation of wave energy conversion devices and that the UK has strong relevant engineering industries that see offshore renewables as an opportunity.

## **3.4 Factors influencing the location of wave generators**

## _3.4.1 Water depth_

Offshore devices have different water depth requirements.  The ‘Pelamis’ device floats on the surface, so the only restrictions in regard to depth would be a minimum depth (e.g. away from surf zones) and a maximum depth governed by the characteristics of the flexible mooring line and the distance from the shore for electricity connection to the grid.  Areas of particular interest to the developers appear to be around the 60m depth contour, presumably because of a particular wave climate at this depth.

‘Wave Swing’ has very specific water depth requirements, and the current pilot project consists of a device 21m in height with the top of the device approximately 10m under the surface.  Therefore, the pilot device (2MW) requires water depths of 30m to make optimal use of the changes in pressure associated with waves passing overhead.  Commercial devices are being contemplated in the region of 6MW and are therefore, assumed to be

larger in height, whilst still requiring a particular height to water depth ratio.  However, prototypes of these units attached by mooring cables to the seabed are being considered, and by alteration of the length of mooring cable the device could be operable in a wider range of water depths.

The ‘Moored Buoy’ floats on the surface, with a large part of its ‘piston structure’ beneath the surface.  The developer of this system has advised that water depths of 50–75m are appropriate for this device.  These limits presumably locate the device in the most favourable wave conditions, whilst reflecting the limitations in regard to mooring cables and distance for connection back to the shore.

The coastline devices, by their nature, are located in relatively shallow water along the coast or very close to or on the shore.

## _3.4.2 Distance from the shore_

The ‘Pelamis’ device will likely be restricted in terms of its maximum distance from the shore by the economics of power supply back to the shore.  The minimum distance from the shore will likely to be governed by the required minimum depth to allow situation of the device in the optimum wave climate i.e. the position of the 60m contours.

The ‘Wave Swing’ device is again constrained by depth of water and this will dictate how far or how near to the shore such a device could be located.

The ‘Moored Buoy’ developers have noted that the device should be located within 5km of the shore, although it is likely that this constraint is largely driven by the high costs associated with power transmission over long distance to the shore rather than any technical requirement.  It is noted however that the required depths (50–75m) will mean that this device will likely be found at least a few kilometres offshore.

This issue is not applicable to the coastline devices.

## _3.4.3 Wave conditions_

Energy from waves is expressed as kilowatts per metre of crest width, and this is generally higher where there is a large fetch in the direction of the prevailing winds.  For these reasons the offshore areas off the Atlantic coasts of Ireland and Scotland have the highest energy resource in Europe. (Clarke and Michael 2001).

The manufacturers of the ‘Moored Buoy’ wave energy device have noted the requirement for the device to be located in areas with a minimum wave energy resource of 28kW/m.  None of the other developers of offshore devices have noted a minimum energy requirement, however it is likely that offshore waters off the coast of west Scotland will provide ample energy for all these devices.

The developers of the ‘Osprey’ onshore wave energy device have noted that in general coastlines with a fetch greater than 400km would generate sufficient wave energy.

## _3.4.4 Seabed/coastal materials_

The ‘Pelamis’ and ‘Moored Buoy’ offshore wave energy devices rely on mooring cables attached to the seabed.  There have been no indications that such moorings will require any specific seabed conditions.

The ‘Wave Swing’ is currently developed on the basis of a pontoon structure to which the ‘floater’ is attached.  This structure is located on the seabed, and will require a flat preprepared area for its location.  It is also likely that some form of attachment to the seabed would be required to ensure that the device couldn’t move.  It is envisaged that seabed scour around the structure may be an issue, and may necessitate the location of this device away from areas of loose sand and clay.

The ‘Osprey’ device is likely to be exposed to fairly large lifting forces due to the compression of air within the column.  Therefore, this device would require being located onto bedrock to allow suitable attachment to resist these forces.

## _3.4.5 Navigation_

The ‘Pelamis’ device rated at 0.75MW is likely to be in the region of 150m in length and 3.5m in diameter, with bigger units increasing in size.  These would be arranged in rows, and it is anticipated that a 30MW wave farm would occupy approximately one square kilometre (Ocean Power Delivery, 2002 - see Figure 3.2).  Such an area would ideally represent an exclusion zone to offshore vessels, and would require marking with buoys and inclusion on the relevant maritime navigation charts.  It is noted that such a wave farm would require to be located away from major shipping lanes, although some re-routing of minor shipping lanes may be possible.

The ‘Moored Buoy’ device rated at 0.25MW is similar in form to existing buoys used to demarcate shipping lanes and indicate obstructions.  Therefore, it is not considered that such devices would necessitate any onerous navigational restrictions, other than possibly a small restriction zone around each device.  However, there is no information in regard to whether or not such devices would be formed into a wave farm type arrangement, with a number of devices located together.

The ‘Wave Swing’ would be located on the seabed, and the top of the structure would be around 10m beneath the surface (based on the prototype device).  This would require a square exclusion area, demarcated by buoys, to be set up around the structure.  Such a device would require being located outside major shipping lanes, as it would provide a hazard to large vessels.

The ‘Osprey’ coastline device is unlikely to cause any navigational constraints.

## _3.4.6 Fishing_

No full Environmental Statements for wave energy devices were available during production of this report. It should be noted that all of these devices are in a relatively early stage of development, with the ‘Limpet’, ‘Wave Swing’ and ‘Moored Buoy’ devices so far having fullscale prototypes installed and tested.  This would indicate that assessing impacts on fisheries, and in particular the disruption these devices may have on fishing activities is also at an early stage.

## _3.4.7 Obstacles on the seabed_

The following areas have been identified as being unsuitable for development of an offshore wave farm:

- Areas around existing undersea pipelines or cables – it is likely that there would be a minimum distance from such obstacles to the nearest mooring cables, specified by the owners of the said pipeline or cable;

- Areas that are or have been used for dumping munitions or hazardous waste – again it is likely there would be a minimum safe distance required to be established, particularly in regard to location of mooring anchors or location of the ‘Wave Swing’ device.

The following areas have been identified as being unsuitable for the development of coastline devices:

- Areas of coast with designations for the protection of offshore flora, fauna, or ecological systems;

- Areas of coast with archaeological significance e.g. wrecks, etc.

## _3.4.8 Military exercise areas_

There are currently a number of sea areas around the UK coastline that have restrictions to vessels because they are used as Navy exercise areas or firing ranges.  A wave farm development would require to be kept at a minimum safe distance from these areas.

## _3.4.9 Radar and communications_

There are only a few small-scale pilot projects involving wave energy devices currently in existence.  Due to their underwater or partially submerged nature it is unlikely that such devices will impact on radar or communications systems.  However, further investigation into such issues would be required.

## _3.4.10 Areas used for dredging_

As discussed earlier, there are currently a number of licences issued by the Crown Estate for the extraction of offshore sands and gravels from designated offshore areas (see section 2.4.12).  These areas would clearly be unsuitable for development of a offshore wave farm due to the constant changes to the seabed caused by extraction, and the attendant effects this would have on mooring anchors or other foundations.

## _3.4.11 Nature conservation areas_

Floating devices such as ‘Pelamis’ and ‘Mooring Buoy’ would likely result in minimal impacts on the local offshore environment.  Mooring anchors are used on both of these devices for attachment to the seabed and therefore the footprint on the seabed is very small.  The only environmental impacts on nature conservation areas would likely be from laying the electricity connection cable, if this is to be buried below the seabed.  However, this type of impact would be experienced regardless of which type of offshore renewable energy is chosen.

Seabed-founded devices such as the ‘Wave Swing’ device would require a larger footprint than floating systems, and accordingly would result in greater disturbance during construction and operation.  This may preclude the location of such devices in sensitive offshore conservation areas.  However, other than the impact of the footprint, there is no information to suggest that any environmental pollution is likely to be caused by the presence of such a device.

The coastline devices would require to be located away from sensitive coastal marine habitats, as there would be disruption of the land/sea interface during the construction of such a device.

Further details of the anticipated natural heritage impacts of schemes are contained in Chapter 12.

## _3.4.12 Ownership_

Seabed ownership is discussed in Section 2.6 and Chapter 8, in relation to wind farms, and those comments would apply to wave energy devices, particularly those that are founded on the seabed.

Shoreline areas for the installation of coastline devices are (particularly in Scotland) likely to be owned by private landowners.  Therefore, agreement for construction access and installation/operation of these devices would require to be progressed with each individual landowner.

## _3.4.13 Grid connection_

Offshore wave energy devices would require the establishment of long lengths of undersea cable to connect them to the grid.  These cables would be brought ashore at a point reasonably close to an appropriate grid connection, to reduce the need for new overhead or underground cabling on land.  A major constraint on the location of such devices off the west coast of Scotland, where the energy potential is the largest in Europe, is that there are few major towns in this area and accordingly the capacity of the grid at coastal locations is unlikely to be able to accept the power from such remote generation (Arup Energy _et al_ 2001).

Currently, wave energy developers are considering connection directly to remote communities from pilot schemes.  However, if wave energy is to be developed to a significant degree, the electrical grid infrastructure will require to be upgraded.

Coastline devices may encounter similar problems to those described above, particularly if they are located on remote coastlines requiring long lengths of cabling to connect to the grid.

In summary, there are technical issues in regard to grid connection, such as capacity, operational procedures, reverse power distribution, and quality of supply.  There are also economic implications attached to either providing long lengths of cabling for a grid connection, or the upgrade required to local infrastructure to allow power from a wave energy development to be accepted onto a local system.

## **3.5 Construction**

Construction of offshore energy devices is not considered to be a significant constraint on their location, as these devices would simply be transported and installed by a vessel with suitable deck space and craning capabilities.  Laying of mooring anchors or preparation of areas of the seabed is relatively straightforward, and would only require avoiding areas previously noted.

Construction of coastline energy devices would rely on access by land or sea for the delivery of construction materials or components.  This may make inaccessible areas of the coastline (e.g. cliff areas) particularly difficult to develop even though energy resources are present.

## **4 TIDAL ENERGY**

## **4.1 Description of the technology**

In the past tidal power conversion was principally thought of in terms of the ‘tidal barrage’ technology.  This technology is still under consideration, for example the DTI has recently commissioned work on a new appraisal of the Severn Barrage Project (Taylor 2002) which examined whether a reappraisal of the barrage project was justified since the studies of the late 1980’s and reported that it was.  More recent approaches to tidal energy conversion fall into two areas, the offshore impoundment method versus the placement of turbine or oscillatory devices in the tidal stream.  Further information on the tidal impoundment concept is available from Tidal Electric’s website (www.tidalelectric.com).  A number of device concepts have been, and continue to be proposed, and there is no consensus on the best approach, or certainty that it has even been identified.

Two principal types of tidal stream energy converters are currently being researched for production of electricity.  The first group uses the tidal stream to rotate blades mounted on a tower, using an arrangement very similar to that used in wind turbines, sometimes referred to as tidal mills.  The second group uses the tidal stream to create an oscillatory motion of hydroplanes.  It is clear that tidal stream devices can be made to work but it still to be demonstrated that this can be done at economically attractive prices for the cost of energy they would generate.

Although this report highlights two tidal stream energy converter demonstration projects in the UK other such projects are being developed elsewhere in Europe and around the world. For example the Norwegians are trialling a tidal mill prototype in the Kvalsundet strait, near Hammerfest, as part of the ‘The Blue Concept’ ecological industrial project (www.etidevannsenergi.com/index.htm).  The idea being to create a tidal power plant, with a maximum of 20 tidal mills generating some 32 GWh per year.

The following two devices have been studied in the production of this report:

- The ‘Marine Current Turbine’ currently being developed by Marine Current Turbines Ltd (www.marineturbines.com).  This device uses the tidal stream to rotate rotor blades located beneath the sea surface.  These rotors are attached to a tower, which is located on a monopile driven or bored into the seabed.  The device generates power in much the same way as a wind turbine, where the rotation of the blades drives a generator that in turn produces electricity;

- ‘Stingray’ is an example of an oscillatory tidal stream power generator (www.engb.com). This is currently being developed by The Engineering Business Ltd.  The device consists of a supporting steel structure with points for attachment to a gravity base.  Attached to this structure are hydroplanes, which when oscillating, drive hydraulic cylinders via highpressure oil, that in turn power a generator.

Ancillary facilities associated with tidal energy devices would be similar to those required for wave energy devices, such as electricity cabling to the shoreline, control buildings, substations and port facilities.

## **4.2 Current Projects**

The ‘Marine Current Turbine’ developers currently have a pilot scheme in operation 1.1km north of Foreland Point, near Lynmouth (N Devon) in the Bristol Channel. An earlier ‘shortterm’ pilot scheme was operated in the Corran Narrow of Loch Linnhe between 1994 and

1995.  Phase 1 (1999 – 2003) of the Foreland Point trial will use a monopile-mounted, experimental 300 kW, single 11 m diameter rotor system.  Thereafter it will be converted to operate with twin 150 kW rotors each of about 8 m diameter (2002 – 2004).  Phase 2 (2003 – 2005) will include connection to the grid and will see the design, manufacture, installation and testing of the first "full size" twin rotor system to be rated at 750 to 1200 kW, which will function with the flow in both directions.  The plan is to complete the initial R&D phase by 2005 and to start commercial installations at that time. It is planned that some 300MW of installations will be completed by 2010.  The final phase (2004-2005) is to install the first small "farm" of tidal turbines interconnected with the Phase 2 system, probably involving 2 to 3 extra units to give an aggregate power for the system of about 2.5 to 5MW - the actual amount depending on how many units and the rated power for the site (www.marineturbines.com/projects.htm).

A pilot scale ‘Stingray’ device (0.15MW) was tested during the summer of 2002 in the Yell Sound, between the Islands of Bigga and Yell in the Shetland Islands (see Section 15.1).

## **4.3 Development Potential**

A developed tidal stream energy conversion technology would be expected to produce electricity at competitive commercial cost with no gaseous emissions or waste products. The successful exploitation of the estimated offshore UK tidal stream resource could make a substantial contribution to the national electricity supply, providing diversity of supply and sustainability in our use of energy.  Studies have shown the UK resource to be between 31 and 58TWh per year.  The report ‘Scotland’s Renewable Resource 2001’ (Garrad Hassan and Partners Ltd 2001) adopted a much more site-specific approach to the selection of appropriate areas for tidal power development, compared to either offshore wind or wave energy.  The Pentland Firth was seen to provide several potential sites.  Others included sites around Islay and Jura, the south end of the Mull of Kintyre, and south of the Mull of Galloway.

ETSU (1993) identified the Pentland Firth as being the single most attractive site in the UK for large-scale tidal current development.  Whilst Michael (2001) suggested it could be a particularly attractive site **if** suitable connections to the grid can be arranged.  Scottish Enterprise has since commissioned a study to establish the environmental feasibility of economic generation of electricity using the tidal current resource of the Pentland Firth.  This study concluded that the long-term benefits would far outweigh the physical, biological and socio-economic disadvantages that may occur and that in the long term the site would be a suitable area for development with adequate consultation and research effort (Bryden, _et al._ 2002).

The UK has the most developed concepts, and further innovative concepts are under consideration.  The UK also has strong, offshore and marine engineering capabilities, mature turbine manufacturing companies, civil engineering and hydraulic engineering industries.  The offshore industry is looking to diversify from its traditional business, and many within the industry see marine renewables as an opportunity where they can exploit skills and experience.

## **4.4 Factors influencing the location of tidal generators**

## _4.4.1 Water depth_

The Marine Current Turbine device has specific depth requirements, and must be located in water between 20 and 30m in depth (measured at low tide).  The current prototype device has rotors 11m in diameter located on a tower that reaches from the seabed to a point a few metres above the sea surface (measured at high tide).

The prototype oscillatory device (Stingray) is approximately 24m in height, and therefore, is likely to have a minimum location depth to achieve total submergence related to the range of the tide and expected wave heights.  The prototype device (0.15MW) is designed to be located in 30m of water, although it is likely that commercial devices would be in the region of 0.5MW, and may therefore, be larger in size and require a greater depth.

It is noted that as technology is developed, larger machines are likely and required depths may increase.  ‘Scotland’s Renewable Resource 2001 – Volume 1 and Volume 2’ produced for the Scottish Executive noted that by 2025 the average depth for tidal energy machines will be around 60m, compared to an expected 30m at 2010.

## _4.4.2 Distance from the shore_

Tidal energy devices are constrained to areas with a sufficient tidal stream resource (discussed below) and a suitable depth related to the size of the machine.  These factors will decide the distances from the shore that will be preferable for such devices.  It is noted however that areas currently identified as having suitable resources are relatively close to the shore, in areas offshore of headland or in tidal races between islands and the mainland. Previous pilot projects on these two devices have all been located within 1km of the shore, and as close as 250m in some cases.

## _4.4.3 Tidal resource_

Tidal energy devices are driven by the flow of water in the oceans created by the effect of the moon and sun’s gravity on these water bodies.  Tidal streams are particularly strong where this movement of water is constrained by terrestrial or seabed topographic features. Areas where a larger than average tidal stream may be found include the area around headlands, in deep water channels between islands and the mainland, between islands and other islands, and in narrow straits at the entrances to sea lochs.

The Current Turbine device requires a mean spring peak tidal velocity of at least five knots (nautical miles per hour), whereas the oscillatory device is currently designed to operate in tidal stream between four and six knots.  Although it is noted that the oscillatory device may be able to be configured so as to operate at higher and lower tidal velocities, these ideas are still under development.

## _4.4.4 Wave conditions_

Review of the technical and operational requirements for these devices has not highlighted any restrictions relating to wave conditions.  Owing to the fact that these devices are located beneath the surface, it is not considered that wave action will have any appreciable effect on their operation.

## _4.4.5 Seabed materials/conditions_

The Current Turbines require a piled foundation of up to 3m in diameter.  Similar constraints apply to piling as previously noted in relation to wind farms.  The developers have noted a preference for a rock or firm geology at any potential site to allow installation.  In addition, they have noted the preference for a flat seabed in the area around the turbine, presumably so as to obtain a relatively smooth and constant flow of water over the turbines.  In an analogy to wind turbines, it is assumed that any irregularities in the water flow past a turbine (eddies, etc.) would increase the turbulence and hence the fatigue loading on a turbine.

The oscillatory energy device has a gravity foundation secured to the seabed with a number of sub-sea anchors.  Again it is likely that such a device would avoid areas of loose sand or clay where it may be difficult to adequately secure a structure to the seabed.

## _4.4.6 Navigation_

The Current Turbine device will have a small amount of the structure above the surface of the sea.  This will presumably provide access to the equipment sited therein.  Rotor diameters of around 16m are expected on a 1MW machine, and there would be two rotors attached to each 1MW machine.  Although no specific comments have been received from the developer, it is anticipated that the passage of large vessels and fishing activities would require to be kept at a minimum safe distance from each device, potentially disrupting fishing activities in the area.  It is not clear whether smaller leisure craft would be able to navigate inside the likely restriction zone for larger vessels.  This would be dependent on their draft, and any surface current anomalies created by the operation of the turbine.  Each turbine or group of turbines would require to be marked on nautical charts, with a stated minimum exclusion zone.  Therefore, the current turbine device would require to be sited away from major and minor shipping routes alike, particularly in regard to maintaining access to existing harbours.

The developers of the oscillatory device have stated that the prototype device would be marked on the surface with a buoy, and the relevant notices to mariners published.  There is enough clearance above the structure such that most leisure vessels can pass safely overhead.  However, the passage of larger vessels and fishing activities would be restricted around the device.  Again such a device should be situated away from major shipping lanes, but would not appear to impede the movement of smaller leisure craft.

## _4.4.7 Fishing_

Both the ‘Marine Current Turbine’ and the ‘Stingray’ devices have undergone environmental studies, with the ‘Stingray’ device also having undergone a full Environmental Impact Assessment.  All of these studies have noted that there are minimal environmental impacts (including those on the fisheries themselves) arising from the construction and operation of these devices.  However, no assessment of their impact on fishing operations has been made.

## _4.4.8 Obstacles on the seabed_

The following areas have been identified as being unsuitable for development of a tidal energy farm:

- Areas around existing undersea pipelines or cables – it is likely that there would be a minimum distance from such obstacles to the device;

- Areas that are or have been used for dumping munitions or hazardous waste – again it is likely there would be a minimum safe distance required to be established, particularly in regard to piling and location of sub sea anchors;

- Areas of seabed that have unsuitable topography (e.g. large rock protrusions, or large changes of bed slope, etc.), and may create irregularities in the flows.

## _4.4.9 Military exercise areas_

A tidal energy farm development would require to be kept at a minimum safe distance from restricted MoD areas.

## _4.4.10 Radar and communications_

There are only a few small-scale pilot projects involving tidal energy devices currently in existence.  Due to their underwater nature it is unlikely that such devices would affect radar or communications systems.  However, further investigation into such issues would be required.

## _4.4.11 Areas used for dredging_

Dredging issues have been discussed earlier.  Designated dredging areas would clearly be unsuitable for the location of tidal energy devices due to the constant changes to the seabed caused by extraction, and the attendant effects this would have on the tidal streams in the area and any mooring anchors.  Refer to section 2.4.12 for information on gravel extraction sites around Scotland.

## _4.4.12 Nature conservation areas_

The offshore current turbines have a relatively small footprint on the seabed and during construction there is likely to be only minor disturbance of the seabed.  Developers have investigated the likely environmental impacts during operation, and no significant impacts have been found.  The blades are not considered to pose a significant threat to wildlife, as they are slow-moving and easily avoided (www.marineturbines.com).  There is no evidence as yet that marine mammals etc. are sucked into the turbines, but this analysis is based upon two pilot scale schemes only, and further research is likely to be required.

The oscillatory device has a larger footprint than the turbine devices presently being designed, and therefore may result in more impact on the seabed as a result of installation. During operation, the character of the remainder of the seabed should be unchanged, and research so far has shown that the device is unlikely to have any significant affects on offshore life.  The unit would be located deeper than most bird species dive (except for the Gannet) but due to the device’s size this is not expected to be a problem.  The developer is currently seeking funds to undertake a hydrophone study, to assess sea mammal populations in the area and examine any impacts from noise created by the device (Entec 2002a).

In summary, it is likely that these devices will be suitable for siting in all but the most sensitive of conservation areas. Further details of the anticipated natural heritage impacts of tidal schemes are discussed in Chapter 13.

## _4.4.13 Ownership_

The ownership issues for tidal devices would be similar to those for wind and wave systems.

## _4.4.14 Grid connection_

Tidal stream devices, based on the sites currently targeted by developers, are all relatively close to the shore compared to offshore wind energy and offshore wave energy sites. Therefore, sub-sea cabling operations would be relatively minor.  However, remote locations would suffer the same problems previously discussed in regard to wave energy grid connection.

## **4.5 Construction**

The construction of tidal energy farms involves either piling or installation of sub-sea anchors, operations that are considered to be relatively straightforward.  The devices

themselves are considerably smaller than those associated with wind turbines, and due to the proximity to the shoreline, construction should be more straightforward.

## **5 OCEAN THERMAL ENERGY CONVERSION (OTEC)**

OTEC uses the natural thermal gradient present between the surface and the depths of the ocean to generate power (www.nrel.gov/otec).  This gradient is created by solar radiation, which is stored in the oceans as heated water.  Some OTEC systems use warmed seawater to evaporate an appropriate fluid (e.g. ammonia) so that the change in pressure created by the vaporisation turns a turbine.  The vapour is then condensed using cold seawater from a greater depth and the process is repeated.  Alternatively, they can use warm seawater directly, which is then flash evaporated to produce steam that drives a turbine; cold seawater is then used to condense the steam and return a cooled seawater discharge back to the ocean.

The system requires a temperature differential of at least 20°C between the sea surface and the water at a depth not greater than 1000 metres.  These conditions are only found in certain areas between latitudes 20[o] S and 20[o] N.  Such a system would not be appropriate for the North Atlantic or the North Sea, simply because the temperature gradient between the sea surface and the deep water is insufficient (typical sea temperatures around Scotland vary from 10°C in the winter to 15°C in the summer).

## **6 LEGISLATIVE AND POLICY BACKGROUND**

## **6.1 Introduction**

This chapter sets out the current policy context for the development of offshore renewable energy generation (February 2003).  There has been rising international concern over the phenomena of climate change and this has driven renewable energy policy over the last decade.  This is reflected in the UK by a positive policy environment for renewable energy generation, motivated by the UK’s commitment to international agreements on reductions in the emissions of climate change gases, and other perceived benefits of renewable energy including the reduction in mining of global fossil fuel supplies, curbing the emission of pollutants such as nitrous oxides and sulphur dioxide, and greater self-sufficiency in energy supply.

## **6.2 International Context**

The United Nations took up the issue of climate change in 1988, and in 1990 the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) confirmed that climate change was indeed a threat and called for a global treaty to address the problem.  The UN General Assembly launched negotiations on a framework convention on climate change and established an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) to conduct these negotiations.  In May 1992 the INC adopted the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, and in June of the same year the Convention was opened for signature at the ‘Earth Summit’ in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.  This came into force in March 1994 and currently 186 governments and the EC are parties to the Convention, the long-term goal of which is to stabilise atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases at ‘safe’ levels.  A series of review mechanisms in the Convention were included to ensure that its commitments could be tightened in the future.  The first of these was the Kyoto Protocol adopted in December 1997, which commits industrialised countries to individual, legally binding targets to limit or reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.  The individual target for the EU is an 8% cut, though this may be redistributed amongst the member states.  The protocol includes provisions for further review of its commitments, and negotiations on targets for the second period are due to start in 2005, by which time industrialised countries must have made ‘demonstrable progress’ in meeting their commitments under the protocol. The UN took up the challenge of renewable energy again at the World Summit, in Johannesburg 2002, on Sustainable Development (www.johannesburgsummit.org).  A key commitment was to diversify energy supply and substantially increase the global share of renewable energy sources in order to increase its contribution to total energy supply.

## **6.3 European Union Climate Change and Renewables Policy**

By 2000, it was clear that action by both Member States and the Community needed to be reinforced if the EU is to achieve the 8% cut in emissions by 2008-2012 as agreed in Kyoto (Natural Power 2002).  The formation of the European Climate Change Programme in March 2000 was tasked with identifying additional policies and measures (as well as an emissions trading scheme) to try and achieve the target.  The EU Renewable Energy Directive was issued in September 2001 and commits Member States to the setting of national targets for consumption of energy from renewable sources in terms of proportion of total electricity.

## **6.4 UK Climate Change and Renewables Policy**

Energy is a reserved matter, and ultimate responsibility for energy policy and its implementation remains with the UK Government.  The Government is currently finalising its Energy White Paper due out in spring  2003, which will consider such things as the energy supply in this country up to 2050 including the issue of renewable energy generation.

In 1998 the UK Government set itself a domestic target for reduction of CO2 emissions beyond its commitment to the Framework Convention on Climate Change, (which was set by the EU as a reduction in a specified range of greenhouse gases of 12.5% by 2008-2012). This target was to reduce carbon dioxide emissions to 20% below 1990 levels by 2010.

The Government published its Climate Change Programme in November 2000, outlining how it was to achieve this domestic target by 2010. The production of energy by renewable sources, the reduction in domestic and business energy consumption and the promotion of sustainable methods of transportation, were all viewed as mechanisms capable of achieving this target. The promotion of renewable sources of energy was seen as a major contributor of greenhouse gas emission reductions within the UK energy sector.

In 2000, the UK Government announced changes in renewable policy, with the Department of Trade and Industry publishing the ‘New and Renewable Energy Prospects for the 21[st] Century – Conclusions in Response to the Public Consultation’.  The objective is that, by 2003, 5% of UK electricity requirements should be met from renewable sources, rising to 10% in 2010, subject to the costs to consumers being acceptable.  The target for Scotland is that 18% of energy should be from renewable sources by this same date (see also next paragraph).

At the recent Earth Summit in Johannesburg, First Minister Jack McConnell expressed his desire to see Scotland lead the way in renewable energy production.  In August 2002, the Minister for Environment and Rural Development, Ross Finnie MSP, indicated that it is the Scottish Executive’s aim to achieve a target of 40% of electricity production to be generated by sustainable means by 2020.  The minister also announced a consultation on the future of renewable energy.  The consultation is taking place in parallel with a consultation on UK energy policy generally, following the UK Energy Review published in February 2002 that was carried out by the Performance and Innovation Unit (PIU) of the Cabinet Office.  The DTI issued _Future Offshore_ , on 22 November 2002, (http://www.dti.gov.uk/energy/leg_and_reg/consents/future_offshore/index.html), which proposes a strategic planning framework as a basis for major expansion of the offshore wind industry.

The current annual supply of electricity in Scotland is approximately 33TWh (Natural Power 2002), of which over 11% is supplied from large scale hydro projects, and over 2% (anticipated to be 3% by 2003) sourced from already commissioned renewable projects and other generation plants that would qualify for grants under the Renewables Obligation Certificates Scheme (see section 6.4.2).  There are indications that Scotland may be asked to increase its 2010 obligations target if the UK’s 10% target for electricity coming from renewables is to be met (Natural Power 2002).  In March 2000 the UK government asked the English regions to assess their renewables resource and establish corresponding regional targets.  The resulting targets were lower than had been hoped for, leading to only 21.2 to 24.9 TWh per year in England of the 39 TWh per year required across the country as a whole by 2010 and would require Wales and Scotland to exceed their current targets for the UK to meet its overall target.

The Non Fossil Fuel Obligation in England and Wales, and the Scottish Renewables Order were initially developed to help promote these policies.  The Renewables Obligation and

Renewables Obligation (Scotland), have now replaced these schemes, but many of the offshore projects currently being considered were supported by the earlier obligations.

## _6.4.1 Scottish Renewables Order (SRO)_

The SRO required public electricity suppliers to contract at least some of their generating capacity from renewable sources.  The emphasis was upon excluding fossil fuels, and technologies such as nuclear, and energy from waste were eligible for inclusion under the scheme.  Projects were approved for inclusion under a series of ‘Orders’.  Three orders were made under the SRO.  Generators submitted proposals under each round of Orders.  Ofgem subjected these to technical and economic feasibility tests.  Contracts were awarded to those proposals that had the lowest bid prices, encouraging more efficient and practical generation of electricity.  Successful projects provided electricity to the suppliers at an above market price, with the deficit funded by the Fossil Fuel Levy.  The premium was paid to recognise the extra cost of small-scale novel energy generation.

## _6.4.2 The Renewable Obligation (Scotland)_

Although energy remains a reserved matter the Utilities Act 2000 devolves the promotion of renewable energy to the Scottish Executive.  This provided Scottish Ministers the power to establish the Renewables Obligation (Scotland) (ROS) through Scottish Statutory Instrument SSI 163 (Anon 2002).

The first consultation paper for the ROS issued in October 2000, explained that it would ‘oblige all licensed electricity suppliers in Scotland to obtain renewables obligation certificates sufficient to cover a specified proportion of the electricity supplied to their customers in Scotland’.  The targets that will increase year on year from 2002 to 2010 are intended to collectively achieve the UK national target of 10% electricity (18% in Scotland) generated from renewable sources by 2010 (Natural Power 2002).

Renewable Obligation Certificates (SROCs in Scotland) will be traded on an open market within the UK as a whole.  Therefore, those suppliers with a deficit of SROCs from their own generation plant may buy SROCs from those suppliers with a surplus, until they meet the renewables obligation for the region they are supplying to.

Renewable energy producing plants that will qualify for SROCs are detailed in Article 8 of the order (Anon 2002).  However, not all plants have been included within this; large-scale hydro-electric projects with a net capacity of more than 20MW, and which were commissioned before April 2002 are omitted, as are certain waste energy projects. Electricity produced from offshore plants would qualify for SROCs providing that the electricity is supplied directly to customers in the UK.

## **7 FUNDING SCHEMES**

## **7.1 Introduction**

There are three main sources of financial support for electricity generated from renewable sources (http://www.dti.gov.uk/renewable/index.html):

- The Renewables Obligation – This is a requirement on licensed electricity suppliers to source a specified proportion of their total sales from renewable sources.  Eligible generation supplied by a licensed supplier to customers in Great Britain attracts Renewables Obligation Certificates (SROCs in Scotland) that may be sold separately from the physical electricity (see section 6.4.2);

- The Emissions Trading Scheme – Renewable energy can, in certain circumstances, be used to help meet emissions reduction targets.  In particular, where individual suppliers over-achieve their obligation and do not wish to sell their ROCs to other suppliers, they may be able to convert their over-achievements to credits measured in CO2 equivalent and trade them under the rules of the scheme;

- Exemption from Climate Change Levy – The Climate Change Levy is levied on nondomestic end users of energy, including electricity.  Electricity from renewables is exempt from the levy and is certified by Levy Exemption Certificates (LECs), which cannot be separately traded from the physical electricity.  The current levy rate is £4.30/MWh, and eligibility is similar to that for the Renewables Obligation.

However, these different methods of financial support cannot all be used at the same time. The basic principle is that emissions reductions in the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) cannot be double counted with emissions reductions achieved through meeting commitments under the Renewables Obligation (www.defra.gov.uk).  The ETS has been designed with the objective of bringing about reductions in emissions of greenhouse gases additional to those that would have resulted from ‘business as usual’.  Emissions that are already covered by a Climate Change Agreement cannot be entered for financial incentive.

The Government has also underpinned their commitment to renewable energy with a series of support schemes designed to bring forward technologies at the demonstration stage. These are being provided through capital grants awarded through the DTI.  The range of investment aid schemes and funding opportunities available are described below (http://www.dti.gov.uk/renewable/index.html).  In addition there are alternative sources of funding which are also highlighted below.

## **8.1 The Role of Crown Estate**

The Crown Estate consists of over 120,000 hectares of agricultural land and substantial blocks of urban property in the UK (England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland) together with 55% of foreshore (over 10,000 km), approximately half of the beds of tidal rivers and estuaries, and almost the entire seabed out to the 12 (nautical) mile territorial limit.  The Marine Estates estate includes the right to explore and exploit the natural resources of the UK continental shelf, with the exception of oil, coal and gas .  The holdings are managed under the Crown Estate Act 1961 by Crown Estate Commissioners (www.crownestate.co.uk).  They have a responsibility to maintain and enhance the capital value of the estate and any potential income from it, whilst having due regard for good management methods and the net surplus is paid to the Exchequer.

In December 2000, the Crown Estate announced a first major round of UK offshore wind farm developments.  Companies could pre-qualify by meeting specific criteria e.g. financial standing, previous experience with renewable energy, demonstrating experience of offshore projects, and an understanding of the environmental constraints and issues that could possibly be important.  Eighteen companies pre-qualified for site development in April 2001 under the Crown Estate procedures and two more were added in 2002.  Developers chose the sites which they were interested in on the basis of relevant factors.

Round One sites are only allowed to install a maximum of 30 turbines in an area of 10 km[2] . Only the one site, made available for development in 2002, in Northern Ireland, following discussions with the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Investment (Northern Ireland) is allowed a maximum of 60 turbines in area of 20 km[2] .  A co-generation project (Ormonde, or East Irish Sea Project) in the Barrow area is a novel development which will produce power from gas reserves and an adjacent wind farm.

Each company had to give a deposit of £300,000, with this paid back to the developer in two stages during the development; £100,000 when the wind monitoring (anemometry) mast has been installed, or six months from the signing of the ‘Agreement for Lease’, whichever is the later.  The remainder of the deposit is refunded when the full lease is entered into or when the agreement is determined, or when the option period expires – whichever is the earlier (Crown Estate _pers. comm._ ).

The Crown Estate has established the Collaborative Offshore Wind farm Research into the Environment (COWRIE) to administer the interest generated from the deposits paid by the developers in the initial tender round (www.crownestate.co.uk, press release 20021225). The panel comprises representatives from the wind energy industry and statutory and voluntary conservation agencies.  It has been decided that this money will be used in paying for generic research into the environmental impacts of offshore wind farms e.g. electromagnetic impacts on fish species, acoustic impacts on offshore mammals, impacts on birds, benthic-feeding habitats, methodology for surveying birds etc.  COWRIE awarded its first research contract in October 2002; the Centre of Maritime and Coastal Studies at the University of Liverpool has been awarded funds to investigate the effects of electromagnetic fields generated by offshore wind farm cables on species such as sharks, skates and rays. These species, which inhabit the waters round the UK, are believed to use electric outputs to capture prey and the earth’s magnetic field for navigation.

Phase two of the scheme whereby Crown Estate would give leases for further wind farms is awaits the outcome of the DTI’s _Future Offshore_ consultation and the SEA for subsequent rounds for the 3 key areas identified in this document.

The leases that are currently in use are for 22 years of operational activity, which when combined to the initial and decommissioning work means that in reality they are nearer to 25.  Decommissioning plans are a requirement of the lease although statutory consents do not at present put conditions on developers for decommissioning although the Scottish Executive are addressing this in light of Robin Rigg.

## _8.2.2 Future Offshore – the consultation_

The likely future importance of offshore wind energy is demonstrated by the fact that the DTI has produced a consultation paper, _Future Offshore_ , to guide its work on this issue: http://www.dti.gov.uk/energy/leg_and_reg/consents/future_offshore/index.shtml.

Following the first round of offshore leases awarded by the Crown Estate the wind industry has shown a keen interest to go further. _Future Offshore_ attempts to ensure the planning framework is right so that developers have the confidence to move ahead and other users of the sea have the reassurance that their interests and those of the environment are being respected.

Before the next round of offshore development takes place certain key issues need to be brought into focus and clarified.  This is because there are many factors which play a part in determining the technical and economic feasibility of development in different locations. These include water depth and access to grid connections, which  mean that some locations will have the capacity for a much greater scale of development than others.  There may be opportunities for sharing offshore cabling, and co-operative planning may be needed to establish onshore grid infrastructure.

The main themes of this consultation are:

- The proposed arrangements for future rounds of development leases, including the detail of the site allocation process and the proposal to focus on strategic areas.

- The specific arrangements for the next round under the existing legal framework.

- The arrangements for a strategic environmental assessment of the three proposed strategic regions prior to the announcement of the next round.

- The proposed changes to the consents process to address specific issues relevant to offshore renewable energy installations.

- The provision and regulation of offshore infrastructure for transmitting electricity.

- Recommendations for a legal framework for future offshore development, to address shortcomings and enable development to take place beyond the limit of territorial waters.

These -main themes are considered further below.

8.2.2.1 The proposed arrangements for future rounds of development leases, including the detail of the site allocation process and the proposal to focus on strategic areas. and The specific arrangements for the next round under the existing legal framework.

_Future Offshore_ examines the possible arrangements for future site leasing or licensing rounds.  It concludes that generally speaking, rounds will have advantages over a continuous process.  It also examines the regional distribution of potentially suitable sites for offshore wind farm development, and proposes that the next development rounds should be concentrated within three regions where there are the largest potentially suitable areas: the North West, the Greater Wash, and the Thames Estuary.  It proposes that the announcement of a competition should be made following the conclusion of this consultation, and a first phase of strategic environmental assessment as explained below.  The target for announcing a competition is April 2003.

The consultation seeks views on a range of aspects of the competition process.  These include the geographic boundaries of the proposed regions, the timing and frequency of rounds, as well as the extent to which developers should be able to propose the size and shape of the area they would wish to explore and ultimately develop.

The proposed regions spread across the boundary of territorial waters and the consultation proposes that a competition for applications for development leases within territorial waters should be supplemented by a competition based on similar principles for exploration licenses beyond the limit of territorial waters.

8.2.2.2 The arrangements for a strategic environmental assessment of the three proposed strategic regions prior to the announcement of the next round.

The potential impacts of future offshore development on all aspects of the environment including the visual impact, as well as the potential impact on other marine industries.  Some of the impacts will be of local significance and will be assessed with development applications through an environmental impact assessment.  However, other impacts will be of more regional significance and some will be linked with the scale of development, such that the impact will be cumulative and related to the scale of development within the region. It will therefore be important to look at the potential impacts on a regional scale to enable decisions to be made as to the acceptable and appropriate level of development within a region.  This needs to be done before an announcement can be made on the next round, as this assessment should play a part in shaping the nature and scale of the round.

A strategic environmental assessment (SEA) is explained and how a regional impact assessment on these lines will be achieved.  An SEA has commenced, focussing on the three strategic regions proposed for the next round, and spanning the boundary of territorial waters.  The first phase of the SEA is due to be completed by early 2003.  During this period the major risks and uncertainties of future offshore development should be identified and work programmes identified or undertaken to provide data to reduce them.  This first SEA work will therefore inform the next round.

8.2.2.3 The proposed changes to the consents process to address specific issues relevant to offshore renewable energy installations.

The consultation identifies areas where specific improvements might be made to the consents process for offshore wind farms.  It proposes how these improvements might be achieved, through streamlining the administration or through legislative change.

## 8.2.2.4 The provision and regulation of offshore infrastructure for transmitting electricity.

The consultation document addresses considerations in relation to the provision and regulation of the offshore electrical cable infrastructure, and requests views on specific proposals.  Offshore cables form an important part of the costs of marine generation.  There may also be significant onshore reinforcement costs when such sites are connected to the electricity networks.  Therefore, ensuring that infrastructure is provided and priced efficiently is important for the success of the offshore wind strategy.

8.2.2.5 Recommendations for a legal framework for future offshore development, to address shortcomings and enable development to take place beyond the limit of territorial waters.

_Future Offshore_ introduces the legal basis for regulating the exploitation of the resource.  It establishes that current legislation fails to provide a firm basis for developments beyond territorial waters, and concludes that new legislation is urgently required in order to enable the huge resource that exists beyond the territorial water limit to be exploited.  It states that the government intends to legislate as soon as possible, but until such legislation comes into force, the ability of developers to obtain rights for development will necessarily be restricted to sites within territorial waters.  In the meantime, however, it may be possible for developers to obtain certain exploration rights to the seabed.  This would have the advantage of enabling developers to conduct exploratory work with an assumption that they would be able to apply for a development licence once the necessary legislation was adopted.

## **8.3 JNCC**

The Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC) is the forum through which the three country conservation agencies – Countryside Council for Wales, English Nature and Scottish Natural Heritage – deliver the statutory responsibilities for Great Britain as a whole, and internationally.  JNCC will endeavour to align the approaches taken by each of the country agencies in respect to renewable energies.

The JNCC is currently working closely with the DTI with regard to the possible new legislation that will need to be introduced to allow wind farms more than 12 miles from the shore. It is the remit of JNCC to cover any nature conservation issues outside of the 12 nautical miles limit, inside the 12 nautical miles the responsibility lies with the national agency i.e. Scottish Natural Heritage.

In general there is a feeling of great confusion over the different aspects of legislation that cover offshore renewable energy developments, with no clear process yet in place. There may be lessons to learn from other countries that have a more developed offshore energy production strategy, such as Denmark, The Netherlands and Australia.

## **8.4 SNH**

SNH is the government body responsible to the Scottish Executive and Scottish Parliament, tasked with providing advice on the natural heritage interests of Scotland out to the 12 mile limit.  The statutory remit of SNH is set out in sections 1, 2 and 3 of the Natural Heritage (Scotland) Act 1991.  Its role is to secure the conservation and enhancement of Scotland’s natural heritage – the wildlife, habitats and landscapes that have evolved in Scotland through the long partnership between people and nature.  SNH’s remit covers nature

conservation, landscape and visual issues, and public enjoyment of the natural heritage. Through a number of statutory and non-statutory consultation procedures, the potential effects of a wide range of marine and coastal civil engineering projects on natural heritage interests are considered by SNH each year.
